Thank you very much, Madam President. Excellencies, this is one part. Country configuration has always been perhaps the most visible for us, and right now what we want to do is much more. The accelerator for us has to be towards the 2030 agenda, and very soon you'll be talking about beyond, but how far can we get with this paradigm shift to sustainable development in this first 15 years that we've had? The mandate delivery is what we are looking to strengthen and not reopen. I think it must be very clear in everything that we do, it is about strengthening that mandate delivery and getting more done with what we can. Domestic resources will be important, leveraging international finance will be important, but here with the system, what can we do? Data is going to be key. We have to fill the data gaps, and so we're working very closely with the HLCM, the MSPC to do so. As Georges has laid out, the 4+9 are really breaking down the areas of contention where we need to get answers and unity as we go forward. The expertise on demand is going to be hugely important to how the UN footprint will work together. The expertise that we have in the UN has been long, I think, undervalued because we've not been able to use it. We have to have the first refusal has to go to the UN system. Cannot just be every consultant that we can find because the UN system cannot provide it and cannot provide it. Why? Because the interoperability is just not there. You will have, with the best will in the world, a major agency of ours who will want expertise from our specialized agencies, not able to give them the rules, the regulations, the model. All of that has to be looked at, and it will require your support in understanding what needs to change to make that happen. So the work of Doreen is incredibly important. Last but not least, as we look at this, there'll be lots of, the oversight is very important. And again, the oversight of the boards has been incredibly important. We had made a few years ago the proposal of the merger of the boards in New York to bring better coherence and oversight across what is a sustainable development agenda. Should you agree to the mergers, then this is a consideration that needs to come up again, because then you will have less of these agencies, it will be much more about the strategy and the UN coherence because those programs will be so much smaller. It will be about programs that countries can leverage, but our support to it will be much more about strategy and UN coherence. Hence then the question of a corporation framework and how we can manage that with accountability to checks and balances and the country project documents are derived from a corporation framework that is fully informed by what we call our country common assessments, which include everything, and particularly the normative, our human rights. All of those have to inform what we do because the outcomes we want are not just the 17 goals, it's the constituencies, women, the human rights at the center, that we don't forget the normative demand that we have of our member states that have all to it. Let me stop there.

Thank you, Amina. Thank you, DSG. I now give the floor to Ms. Ayaka Suzuki, Director in the Executive Office of the Secretary General, who will deliver remarks on behalf of Mr. Guy Ryder, Under-Secretary-General for Policy.

Great. Thank you very much, Madam President. Excellency, thank you so much for joining us today, despite the tricky road and sidewalk conditions, and for engaging so actively on the UN80 initiative. I believe you will all agree that today's presentations that you just heard demonstrate both the breadth and ambition of the work underway. In several areas across the UN80 Initiative, this is the first time that the UN system is truly coming together in such a comprehensive manner to address issues collectively. And before we turn to you to listen to your reflections, please allow me to say a few words on where we stand in managing the UN Aid Initiative overall. So you will recall that we started the UN Aid Initiative with three work streams. On the first work stream, we have made very significant progress. The efficiencies proposals put forward in a 2026 revised estimates for the Secretariat received broad endorsement from you, the Member States. And in your budget resolution, you also expressed strong support for the UNAIDS initiative as a whole and called on us to maintain its momentum. Thank you. We also took careful note of the specific requests contained in the budget resolution, and please rest assured that we are taking those requests into account as we move forward. On the second work stream, as mentioned by the President of the General Assembly, on the mandates, there is also very encouraging progress. Many of you are actively contributing to the work of the informal ad hoc working group on mandates. As you know, the working group has now entered its production phase, which is expected to conclude by 31st March. The co-chairs, ambassadors, Wallace and Schwelger of Jamaica and New Zealand have introduced a zero draft resolution on mandates on 8th of January that covers the full mandate life cycle and looks at systemic issues across mandating bodies, UN system pillars, and entities. And they have indicated that the second draft will be circulated around 23rd February. And as I said, with a view to concluding the work by the end of March. We believe the work being undertaken by this working group has the potential to make a meaningful difference in how mandates are created, implemented, and reviewed. And we stand ready to support your work in any way that may be useful. Now, turning to the third work stream on structural changes and program realignments. As you will recall, overall, we are advancing 31 work packages and about 90 actions across the three work streams in partnership with over 50 UN system entities. And you have heard today about some of the work currently underway, and you will continue to hear more in the weeks and months ahead. And in each briefing every month, we will deep dive into few work packages like you have heard today. And to help you track our progress across all work packages, we now have an updated online dashboard available at un80actions.un.org. Let me repeat, un80actions, one word with 80 in numbers, .un.org. The dashboard covers all work packages and all actions in the UNAD Action Plan across the three work streams. For each of these, and you see the screenshot of what the dashboard looks like. So for each of this, the dashboard shows who is leading, who is part of the team, and what the status is, where decisions have been taken, or where work is ongoing. The purpose is to be transparent on actions, responsibilities, and timelines. The dashboard already contains a wealth of information across all the work packages on the work we are undertaking and the timelines we are setting ourselves. We will update the dashboard as our proposals take shape. We would encourage you to spend some time familiarizing yourself with the dashboard, as I believe it will be a valuable tool for all the colleagues who are contributing to the success of UN80. And we would, of course, be happy to organize a technical briefing as we have done with the Mandate Registry Dashboard as well. So let me also take this opportunity to give you a few additional indications on where and when we expect decisions will have take will have to be taken. At the outset, let me again provide assurances that all actions will be undertaken in accordance with the applicable rules and procedures as set out in the Charter, as well as the decisions, resolutions and established practice of the competent intergovernmental organs. As I had mentioned in my presentation on the, not my presentation, but under Secretary General Ryder's presentation on the UN AIDS Action Plan in November, the exact contour of the proposals will ultimately determine which decisions are required and where those decisions will be taken. Some of the proposals will be reflected in the 2027 program budget proposals. Others will require separate legal instruments, including General Assembly resolutions. For example, if the outcome of the merger assessment is to move forward with merger proposals, they will be referred to the General Assembly for consideration and approval. Madam President, Excellencies, looking at the weeks ahead, let me give you a sense of some key dates we are working towards. The Secretariat has started work on the programme budget for 2027, which we will present to you in the spring. The executive boards of UNDP, UNFPA, UNOPS, UNICEF and UN Women will meet in February and then again in June. the Deputy Secretary General will be presenting progress on some of the work packages under her leadership to the boards. In May, we will hold our next Chief Executives Board for coordination meeting. That will be a key moment for the system to adopt key proposals developed under the UN80 initiative. At the invitation of the President of the General Assembly, we will hold consultations with you each month on specific proposals. For our next briefing scheduled for the end of February, we hope to welcome Under Secretary General Tom Fletcher to discuss the Humanitarian Compact, subject to confirmation. In addition to these monthly opportunities for consultations, individual work package leads will also be seeking Member States' guidance on the proposals they are developing. And thank you. We look forward to your comments and questions. Thank you, Madam President.

I thank the Director. I now open the floor for comments or questions to the very, very detailed briefings, for which I'm very thankful. This meeting will not have a pre-established list of speakers. Delegations wishing to take the floor are invited to press the microphone button. Time limit will be strictly enforced through an automatic microphone cutoff. A timer will be projected on the screen. Madam President, it's my honor to make this statement on behalf of the member states of the Gulf Cooperation Council, the UAE, the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, the Sultanate of Oman, the State of Kuwait, the State of Qatar, as well as my country, the Kingdom of Bahrain. At the outset, I would like to extend my most heartfelt thanks to you. Thank you for organizing this important meeting devoted to the UN80 initiative. I thank Ms. Amina Mohammed and the ITU Secretary General, Ms. Bogdan-Martin, and the Special Advisor on Reforms, as well as the Executive Director of UNOPS. Thank you all of you for your enlightening briefings. Madam President, the UNAT Initiative is constantly committed to exploring means and ways of strengthening the efficiency and effectiveness of the working methods to implement our mandates and to proceed to a strategic review of the structural reforms and the realignment of programs. And this in order to support efforts seeking to strengthen the UN system, respecting the principles of the UN Charter and the Pact for the Future. The states of the Council We affirm our support to the Secretary-General's UNAT initiative as one of the efforts being made to strengthen the efficacy of it and to reduce overlap and to improve the capacity of our organization to discharge its mandates, in particular in the face of emerging challenges. We underscore the absolute need to consolidate the principles of transparency and accountability in this regard. We welcome the launching of the UNAT indicators platform as well as the progress made by the initiative in its implementation phase. In this regard, we feel that the adoption of a realistic and flexible approach for the implementation timeline and strengthening transparency and accountability principles are a key pillar to make this initiative focused on its trajectory. Madam President, when it comes to structural changes and the realignment of programs within the UN system, The States of the Council underscore the need for this Council to be part of a well thought out, progressive approach that respects the highest standards of effectiveness, efficacy and good stewardship of resources whilst respecting the principle of equitable geographic representation. By way of conclusion, the states of the Gulf Cooperation Council believe that providing complete access to proposals and ensuring interactive participation from member states are essential elements to ensure that this initiative is a success. The Secretary General's initiative right now is the only way that will enable us to make progress in the strengthening of multilateralism and to achieve the desired results effectively. Thank you.

I thank the distinguished representative of Bahrain, speaking on behalf of the Gulf Cooperation Council. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Australia, speaking on behalf of CANZ.

Thank you, President, and can I express particular appreciation for the quality of our briefings this morning, Deputy Secretary-General, but other colleagues as well. And I think I might make this comment in my national capacity before my prepared remarks, but I think the value of the data that we have seen this morning and the conversation that we have seen this morning gives all of us confidence that we actually do have a path forward. We obviously have work to do, but I think every one of us in this room should walk away with the sense that actually we have a concrete project with well-defined objectives and a clear pathway forward. And I thank you very much indeed for that. I think it's tremendously important that we and our capitals have that confidence. It's clear that we'll only achieve effective reform by having clear expectations, measurable progress, transparent communication, sustained commitment, and disciplined follow-through. The regular briefings, including this morning, of course, are a critical contribution to this. From a CANS perspective, we have four points we would like to make today. First, we must collectively remain focused on our shared goal of reform that builds a UN able to respond to current and future challenges in line with the core mandate of the United Nations, but very importantly, the three pillars that we are all committed to. We welcome the Secretary-General's objective of a leaner system that delivers more effectively, more coherently, and with greater impact amid shrinking resources and rising needs. We will continue to back actions that advance it and support an ongoing culture of efficiency. At the same time, we will uphold the key normative mandates and institutional architecture that are foundational to effective delivery and meaningful impact. Member states and the United Nations system are both accountable for delivering concrete results, and we need to work together. In this vein, Cairns continues to encourage the Secretary-General to implement those proposals that lie within his existing authority and which he's able to prosecute without further bureaucratic processes involving multiple member states. Second, CAN stresses the importance of full transparency throughout this process. And as my opening remarks mentioned, I think very much that the type of briefing we've received this morning responds to that call. Knowing what decisions are needed, who they are needed by, which member states, governing bodies, or the Secretary-General, and when they're needed is imperative to hold ourselves and the UN system accountable for timely action under the UN80 initiative. We also support the use of tools that enable us to track progress and maintain accountability, and very much welcome the advice we received this morning on the tools that are being put in place to enable us to do that. The online UNAD dashboard, including the identification of action leads, is critical to assessing concrete progress and ensuring ongoing transparency, and again, we very much welcome the advice we've received. Third, reforms must continue to be developed in consultation with member states and UN stakeholders, and we look forward to receiving proposals for country and regional level reforms. They offer promise of a more effective and impactful UN and will have significant implications on how the system operates on the ground. And it's essential that they be shaped through broad and meaningful engagement and consultation. It will also be important that proposals are flexible enough to be effective in the wide variety of regional, sub-regional and national contexts, and are appropriately consulted and tested with member states and other key stakeholders to ensure they can deliver on their objectives in different settings. Further, it's vital that all relevant UN entities take a system-wide perspective on these reforms and get behind useful, practical proposals that can deliver greater impact. Finally, CANS looks forward to receiving further information on the timeline and processes to continue detailed assessment of proposed mergers, including between UNDP and UNOPS, and UNFPA and UN Women. We reiterate the importance of decisions on these and other proposals being based on a robust business case focused on achieving operational efficiencies and enhanced effectiveness and do not involve a reopening of the core mandates of entities. The executive boards are key decision makers as well as a crucial source of expertise and must be closely engaged in this process. Member states will also require adequate time to consider the merits of these and other proposals in depth. President Cairns remains committed to working with the Secretariat and all member states to ensure UNAD delivers a more coherent and effective UN. Thank you so much.

I thank the distinguished representative of Australia speaking on behalf of Cairns. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the European Union speaking on behalf of the EU member states, followed by China and Mexico.

Thank you, Madam President, Madam Deputy Secretary General, distinguished colleagues. I have the honor to deliver this statement on behalf of the EU and its member states. The candidate countries North Macedonia, Montenegro, Ukraine, the Republic of Moldova, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Georgia, as well as Armenia and Andorra, align themselves with this statement. Thank you, Madam President, for gathering us today to hear such insightful briefings on the UNAD initiative. And I agree with the colleague from Australia that these have been very, very informative and insightful indeed. We hope, of course, that the slides can be shared, maybe on the dashboard, because it was very hard to see them from up here. We thank the briefers for sharing their perspectives from across the UN system, and also USG Ryder and the UNAD task force for their continuous efforts. UNAD requires a sustained collective effort, and we highly appreciate the expertise and valuable support in this exercise that we have seen from the briefers today. In December, the General Assembly adopted the UN budget by consensus as the first step in the implementation of the UNAD initiative, clearly acknowledging the interconnected nature of its three work streams. The European Union welcomes this opportunity to exchange views on structural alignment and system-wide coherence in parallel with the substantive work in the Intergovernmental Working Group on work stream 2. Taken together, these processes are mutually reinforcing and should continue to inform and strengthen each other. And in this respect, allow me to highlight our main considerations on the proposed structural reforms and program realignment in Workstream 3. First, we support strengthening the role, efficiency, and effectiveness of the UN Resident and Humanitarian Coordinators across the system. and empowering them with clear authority, adequate tools and accountability at the country level to ensure an integrated approach, streamlined delivery and results-oriented coordination. The road ahead is clear, and now it's time to ensure that the Resident Coordinators are enabled to truly lead the UN at country level and ensure system-wide efficiency and effectiveness while avoiding duplication and fragmentation at country level. This step, as we know, requires support from the entire UN development system, including UN funds, programmes and agencies. Second, the UN must continue to uphold, defend and adequately fund human rights across all pillars, as stated in the Charter. We look forward to receiving more details on the proposed Human Rights Group's mandate, composition and reporting lines, including how it will ensure that human rights considerations are systematically integrated across UN policies and support, and how it will align with the Pact for the Future. And third, sustainable development, human rights and gender equality remain central to the work of the EU. We stand ready to exploring the potential of the proposed mergers of UNDP and UNOPS and UNFPA and UN Women through meaningful engagement with the executive boards, and assessments based on thorough and independent analysis. It's essential that any potential merger preserves the existing mandates of these agencies. We stand ready to engage in further consultations to ensure that any merger proposal does not dilute existing mandates agreed by member states, but rather aims to reinforce their implementation. A transparent timeline on when the assessments will be shared with member states would be appreciated. Madam President, Coherence between New York, Vienna, Nairobi and Geneva is essential as the work streams progressively converge. Enhanced coordination and system-wide coherence for increased efficiency stand at the very core of our reform efforts. Yet efficiency must never come at the expense of human rights capacity. We expect reform to strengthen and not weaken accountability and protection. The leadership across the entire UN system must continue to promote a culture of change and efficiency, which should be anchored in an updated action plan with main milestones and timelines. Our collective ambition will be critical not only to ensuring continuity of reform, but also to consolidating gains, sustaining momentum, and delivering lasting impact. The United Nations can always count on the support of the European Union and its member states to produce meaningful and long-lasting reforms in the system. And I thank you, Madam President.
I thank the distinguished representative of the European Union. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of China.

Madam President, I thank you for convening this meeting. And I thank TSG, Amina Mohammed, and other briefers for their presentations. The UN 80 Initiative is a crucial pathway to enhancing the quality, efficiency, and effectiveness of the UN and for vitalizing its authority and vitality. Through the concerted efforts of member states, the Secretariat, and other stakeholders, this reform has continued to advance in depth and substance with the positive progress. The task ahead remains demanding. I wish to share three observations. First, consolidate existing achievements, measures to enhance for no efficiency and effectiveness have been put in place. Member states, through difficult negotiations, have set out new requirements for the UN to improve cost effectiveness in policy and resource. The next step is to effectively implement reform measures, foster a culture of efficiency effectiveness, allocate valuable resources to member states where already agendas and mandates advance the work of the three pillars in balanced manner. The secretaries of member states should continue to strengthen communication, close collaboration, and to enhance overall effectiveness. Second, serve the broad membership Mandate implementation reviews and structural reforms concern the interests and needs of member states. Any measure introduced must place broader membership, in particular developing countries, at their center. Development reform should fully leverage the center of DESA with enhanced internal coordination and coherence within the secretariat. Other development agencies should forge synergy and complementarity. Regional level reforms must reflect the requirements of countries in the regions concerned. Reform of the RC system should focus on development mandates, avoid addition of mandates from the peace and security pillar. Actions to improve mandates must reflect the voice of developing countries. Third, observe appropriate working methods. We need to strengthen system-wide approach. Reforms should avoid to the greatest extent possible overlapping of mechanisms and creating additional resources requirements. Structural reform in the development area should comprehensively consider human, financial, and material factors to ensure staff morale and operational effectiveness. We expect the Secretary to draw on past lessons learned and to take a long-term view in proposing a scientific and prudent reform plan for the system. Reform outcomes should be thoroughly discussed, reflect consensus, be adopted by consensus among Member States. China is ready to work with Member States to advance reform that serves long-term development of the UN and the common interests of all Member States, we look forward to receiving relevant timelines and specific proposals. Thank you, DSG, and thank you, Madam President.
I thank the distinguished representative of China. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Mexico, followed by Brazil and Morocco.

Thank you very much, Madam President. Mexico wishes to thank the Deputy Secretary-General, Ms. Amina Mohammed, and the whole of the UN team for all of their efforts to make headway with the UNAT initiative. Thank you also for the transparency with which you have led this process and the progress made in the two first phases of the work. On axis 1, we welcome the approval of the ordinary budget for the United Nations and the measures of the Secretary-General to improve the efficiency of the Organization. This is the first step in the right direction in the implementation of the UNAT initiative. On the implementation of mandates, which is the second part, my country, Mexico, is participating actively in the negotiations for the relevant resolution in order to drive cultural change for the implementation of mandates for member states and thus avoid duplications. Lastly, Mexico reiterates that the three pillars of the UN IT initiative are closely linked to each other and we underscore the importance of ensuring that they are implemented throughout the United Nations system. In this regard, we are grateful for the presentations on commitment to the UN IT initiative on the part of the Secretary General of the International Telecommunication Union, ITU, and also from the Secretary General of the UN Office for Services and Projects. Mexico is looking forward to proposals related to the knowledge on demand mechanisms and to the setting up and configuration of the UN country teams and will give due consideration to these. Thank you very much.
I thank the distinguished representative of Mexico. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Brazil.

Thank you, Madam President, and many thanks to the DSG and the briefers. I'll make very brief general comments. Since its launch, Brazil has been supportive of the UN80 initiative. We fully align ourselves with the objective of ensuring a United Nations that is capable of responding effectively to today's challenges in a fast-changing world. Institutions must be able to adapt swiftly if they are to remain relevant and effective. Reform, therefore, is not an option but a necessity, and UNAD is a key contribution in that direction. Brazil is also fully aligned with the strategy of strengthening the Resident Coordinator system, which has been working very well in aligning the UN system with Member States' priorities. At the same time, not all reforms are the same, and together we must devise what changes best serve our shared goal of building a stronger organization, one that helps states sustain and promote multilateralism. UNHCR should at all times preserve the balance among the three pillars of the United Nations, peace and security, development, and human rights, as enshrined in the charter. These pillars were conceived together because they are inseparable. Any reform effort that weakens one pillar risks undermining the UN as a whole and the interests of the vast majority of member states. We need appropriate metrics and statistical monitoring mechanisms to track and assess the effects of the initiative across the three pillars. Brazil fully supports efforts for much deeper coordination and rationalization across agencies, funds, and programs. where this leads to genuine efficiency gains and better use of scarce resources. Such efforts must not come at the expense of mandates, the creation and review of which are the exclusive prerogative of member states. The consolidation of entities must never dilute or implicitly eliminate mandates unless so expressly decided by the membership. We remain ready to engage constructively to ensure that this initiative delivers a more responsive organization firmly anchored in the principles of the Charter and in the interests of all Member States. Thank you.
I thank the Distinguished Representative of Brazil. I now give the floor to the Distinguished Representative of Morocco, followed by Indonesia and Armenia.

Thank you very much, Madam President. Morocco wishes to thank you for convening this briefing and expresses its appreciation to the Deputy Secretary General for her leadership, as well as to all the distinguished briefers for their clear and informative presentations. In this regard, I would like to highlight the following points. First, any reflection on structural realignment must respect the intergovernmental character of the organization. Two, structural realignments must primarily aim at enhancing the organization's capacity to deliver, particularly in developing countries and mainly in the builder of development. Three, any reconfiguration, including under UN country team reconfiguration, should be based on its previous experience, successes, and challenges, and cooperation with countries. Four, mechanisms such as expertise on demands needs to reflect regional and country-specific context, particularly in setting where the United Nations has a central role. Five, we must ensure that structural adjustments do not weaken the institutional visibility and political weight of the development pillar, which remains central to the priorities of development countries. Finally, Morocco looks forward to the upcoming briefers and remains committed to contributing to the shared objective of strengthening a United Nations that is more effective, more coherent, and more responsive to the needs of its member states. I thank the distinguished representative of Morocco. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Indonesia.

Thank you, Madam President, for convening this important briefing. And I also wish to thank Madam Deputy SG and all briefers for the insightful presentation. Allow me to echo the previous speaker to have the presentation shared with member states. In an increasingly complex global landscape, coherence across the UN system is not only desirable, but essential. We must ensure that reforms lead to more integrated, responsive, and effective support for countries in responding to current and future challenges. Second, we reaffirm the importance of engaging member states' concern on UN Country Team reconfiguration. The principles of national ownership and alignment with country priorities must remain at the heart of the Country Team reconfiguration. And third, we also highlight the importance of embedding a culture of continuous improvement. While regular briefings are vital, they should be complemented by mechanism that allow for adaptive implementation learning from experience, and timely course improvement. The UNAT dashboard, in our view, should serve not only as a monitoring tool, but also as a platform for constructive feedback and shared learning. Could the briefers elaborate on how relevant member states will be meaningfully consulted in shaping the reconfiguration of the UN Country Team under Work Stream 3? And second, in light of the emphasis on transparency and accountability, how will the UNAT dashboard be designed to incorporate feedback from program countries, particularly in reflecting on the ground realities and informing adaptive implementation? Thank you, Madam President.
I thank the distinguished representative of Indonesia. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Armenia, followed by the United Arab Emirates and Zimbabwe.

Madam President, we thank you for convening this meeting. We also thank the Deputy Secretary-General and other briefers for sharing the current state of play and the perspectives on structural reforms and programmatic realignments across the UN system. We are pleased to note the advancement of discussions around the work packages of the Action Plan and Work Stream 2, in a spirit of forward-looking, coherent, and mutually reinforcing exercise, aimed at upscaling the organization and its entities, and create synergy between normative and operational work. We are strongly convinced that both progress and setbacks in the area of international peace and security and sustainable development are conditioned by our ability to uphold fundamental human rights and promote prevention agenda. We hope that the proposed new human rights group will be fit for purpose and strengthen the human rights pillar of UN. Adequate financing of the human rights pillar and equipping it with human resources is important to ensure its regular mandated activities and ability for early response to the most acute cases of gross human rights violations. We recognize the key role of resident coordinators in enhancing coordination, coherence, and efficiency of UN country teams to ensure the nexus between peace, humanitarian, and development efforts. We also stress the importance of transparency and accountability at our country level to ensure that the programmatic activities are aligned with the host country's needs and priorities. Adequate financing, enhancing overall efficiency, coherence, and responsiveness of the UN development system shall be in the center of our discussions and deliberations. These efforts involve the need to avoid duplications and create synergies in delivery of programmatic activities. In this context, we welcome the opportunity to explore the potential benefits of a consolidated institutional arrangement between UNDP and UNOPS, with a view to leveraging UNDP, complemented by UNOPS operational capacities. Madam President, to conclude, let me express our readiness to engage in the UN80 process with a view to strengthen the capacities and efficiency of the organization based on the recommendations of three work streams and the deliberations set to be converged towards a unified reform package. And I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Armenia. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the United Arab Emirates.

Madam President, at the outset, I would like to thank you for convening this important meeting. I also wish to thank the Deputy Secretary-General and the briefers for their insightful presentation. This is an historic opportunity to ensure that the organization is focused, coherent, and able to deliver results where it adds the greatest value. We must not squander it. For the initiative to succeed, it must strengthen all three pillars of the United Nations work in a balanced and integrated manner. Efforts must be made to reduce duplication, clarify roles, and strengthen system-wide alignment based on the comparative advantage of each part of the UN system. The need for streamlining is particularly evident in the humanitarian sector. Effective humanitarian action is highly dependent on Operational coherence reforms that integrate and coordination and strengthen country level authority are therefore essential enablers of impact in the field. At the same time, bold reform must be pursued in a transparent and inclusive manner, firmly anchored in member state ownership and aimed at strengthening the effective implementation of mandate entrusted by member states. We also encourage the appropriate use of new technologies to enhance transparency and reduce duplication across the UN's work. We welcome recent efforts to enhance transparency through improved data, indicate and digital tools, and encourage the Secretariat to continue to build on these tools. Madam President, the UN80 Initiative will ultimately be judged by the depth of positive change it delivers. This will require political will, discipline, and a shared commitment to improving the organization's delivery on the ground where it matters most. The UAE stands ready to engage constructively to ensure that the initiative results in a more coherent, efficient, and effective United Nations. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of the United Arab Emirates. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Zimbabwe, followed by Romania and Japan.

Thank you, Madam President. We welcome the convening of this meeting and commend your leadership and commitment to transparent, and inclusive engagement on reform. We thank the Deputy Secretary-General and the team for the comprehensive briefings, and we acknowledge the progress achieved across the three workstreams in laying the foundations for a more agile, responsive, and coherent United Nations system. We will continue to study these inputs from the Secretariat carefully recognizing that this reform process remains a work in progress. Madam President, allow me to raise two focused reflections.
